title: Globalive’s Anthony Lacavera wants to buy Freedom Mobile back if Telus takeover proceeds
html:
Former founder and CEO of Freedom Mobile, Anthony Lacavera, says Globalive will make an offer to acquire Freedom Mobile out of the Quebecor-Telus consolidation.Christopher Katsarov/The Globe and Mail

Several years ago, Anthony Lacavera tried and failed to buy back the wireless carrier he had founded back in 2008. Now, a proposed takeover of Telus Corp. T-T by the carrier’s current owner, Quebecor Inc., QBR-B-T has inspired him to try again.

Mr. Lacavera, the chairman of Toronto-based investment company Globalive Corp., is courting prospective investors in the hopes that Ottawa will require Quebecor to divest Freedom Mobile, Canada’s fourth-largest wireless carrier, should its acquisition of Telus proceed.

“Globalive will make an offer to acquire Freedom Mobile out of the Quebecor-Telus consolidation,” Mr. Lacavera said in an interview, calling his company “best positioned” on account of having founded Freedom’s predecessor, Wind Mobile.

He’d also be interested in picking up any assets divested should BCE Inc.’s Bell Canada be the buyer, instead. The Globe and Mail has reported that Bell has held preliminary discussions with Telus and hired financial and legal advisers as it explores its options in the wake of Quebecor’s proposal.

“We continue to have low levels of innovation and customer experience and very high prices, and so it’s clear more competition continues to be needed. And this transaction is only going to serve to reduce competition unless the government ensures we have a framework for more competition,” Mr. Lacavera said.

Any new competitor in the market would likely require the support of government, new network-sharing policies and significant investment to build out telecom infrastructure.

Mr. Lacavera declined to name the price he’d pay for the carrier or the prospective investors that he’s spoken to. While he has not yet engaged Quebecor or Telus, he said he has held “informal” talks with regulators about his intention to re-enter the market.

Last week, Quebecor went public with its non-binding proposal to acquire its larger rival, Vancouver-based Telus, arguing that the combined companies would be better able to invest in networks, improve telecom offerings for consumers and compete against global tech giants, such as Elon Musk’s Starlink.

Wind Mobile was renamed Freedom Mobile in 2016, after the company was acquired by Shaw.Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press

While Telus has a fiduciary duty to review the proposal, the company’s executives and special board committee say the offer undervalues its assets, proposes an unworkable dual-class share structure and would face significant regulatory hurdles. Even without Telus’s support, Quebecor could attempt to push its deal through in a hostile takeover – a direct offer to Telus shareholders.

Quebecor has not yet said what remedies – for instance, divestitures to counteract anti-competitive effects – it might be willing to offer Ottawa to secure its approval and mitigate concerns about consolidation. But analysts and competition lawyers have suggested that in any deal, hiving off a major telecom asset, such as Freedom or Telus’s wireless assets, could be a solution.

Freedom’s predecessor, Wind Mobile, was one of three wireless upstarts that emerged when Ottawa set aside airwaves for new entrants in a 2008 spectrum auction. The two others, Public Mobile and Mobilicity, were later acquired by Telus Corp. and Rogers, respectively.

Globalive’s financing, from Egyptian billionaire Naguib Sawiris, became a thorny issue for Wind. The carrier’s launch was delayed because the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission determined that Globalive did not meet Canadian ownership rules.

The decision was later overturned by the federal government, but the issue resurfaced in a legal battle that was appealed all the way to the Supreme Court.

The court declined to hear the case, handing Wind a victory. But in 2011, Mr. Sawiris decided to sell his stake in Wind to Russian-controlled VimpelCom Ltd.

A few years later, in 2014, the carrier’s new owners decided not to back its attempt to buy additional spectrum, forcing Mr. Lacavera to recapitalize the company with funding from Canadian and U.S. private equity investors, who snapped it up for a bargain price of $300-million.

Fourteen months after that, the consortium sold Wind to Shaw for $1.6-billion. Shaw renamed the carrier Freedom Mobile.

Mr. Lacavera maintains that he didn’t want to sell Wind. “I would have never sold the company. I would be 90 years old on my deathbed owning that company,” he once told The Globe and Mail.

Then, in 2023, Freedom was sold again, when Ottawa forced Rogers Communications Inc. to divest it as part of its $20-billion takeover of Shaw. Mr. Lacavera offered $3.75-billion for the carrier and launched a months-long public relations campaign. He even tried bypassing Rogers and taking his offer directly to Shaw, but ultimately lost out to Quebecor, which offered considerably less: $2.85-billion.

Since then, Freedom’s growth has been on a tear. After acquiring the brand, Quebecor expanded services across the country and has outpaced its larger rivals on wireless subscriber growth by maintaining lower wireless prices, part of a series of commitments it made to Ottawa in 2023.

Quebecor inherited about 1.82 million wireless subscribers with the Freedom acquisition, bringing its total, including existing wireless operations, to about 3.61 million as of June 30, 2023. That total has jumped to 4.62 million subscribers as of Sept. 30 this year.

And since the beginning of 2023, Quebecor’s share price has risen about 100 per cent, while its rivals Rogers, Telus and Bell have seen theirs drop by about 20 per cent, 41 per cent and 47 per cent, respectively, over the same period.

Should Mr. Lacavera succeed in acquiring Freedom, he hopes to build a “pure-play” wireless operator – one that, unlike Canada’s largest incumbents, does not also own legacy assets that weigh on the balance sheet and constrain the rollout of future technologies.

For instance, a company that owns extensive wireline infrastructure may be less likely to offer fixed wireless internet, which doesn’t require a direct physical line into the home, as it would compete with that legacy network, he said. Fixed wireless – which he hopes to offer – typically can’t reach the same speeds as a wireline connection but can be provided more cheaply.

“We have to have a pure-play wireless operator in Canada. We can’t go another round of having cable companies and phone companies own all the wireless companies,” he said.

But running Freedom comes with a wide set of challenges. One is the expense of building out physical infrastructure – one motivation behind Quebecor’s proposal to buy Telus.

Moreover, Freedom Mobile is currently reliant on network-sharing agreements outside the urban areas where Freedom Mobile owns its own network, and on benefits to new entrants that could soon expire.

The current policy, intended to promote competition by giving new entrants a foothold while they build networks, caps the access fees that telecoms pay to rivals to offer service by “piggybacking” on their infrastructure.

That government-set fee structure is set to expire in 2030. Unless the sunset is extended, companies will have to negotiate access fees commercially, meaning higher access costs that could change the economics of growth.

Any deal would require “sufficient facilities and spectrum to continue to grow it,” Mr. Lacavera said, as well as government action to ensure ready access to towers and roaming agreements.

Mr. Lacavera, meanwhile, has set out to disrupt another industry that he characterizes as an oligopoly: Banking.

Last year, a consortium led by Globalive acquired Wealth One Bank of Canada, a small, Toronto-based Schedule I bank subject to a federal government divestiture order.
summary: Founder is courting prospective investors as Quebecor-Telus consolidation talks continue
